## P99 — EXPANDED ARCHITECTURE CONTENT


Trade-off analysis: hexagonal-architecture for payment. Quality attributes: availability (99.99%), latency (p99 < 200ms), scalability (10k TPS), security (PCI-DSS Level 1), cost (<$50k/month). Architecture hexagonal-architecture scores: availability 9/10 (active-active multi-region), latency 8/10 (in-process calls vs network hops), scalability 7/10 (horizontal with partitioning), security 8/10 (defense-in-depth layers), cost 6/10 (infrastructure complexity). Alternative: simplified layered architecture scores availability 7/10, latency 9/10, scalability 5/10, security 7/10, cost 9/10. Recommendation: hexagonal-architecture for core domain, layered for bounded contexts where scalability is not critical.

Technology selection: inventory event-driven-architecture implementation technology. Candidates: 0: TypeScript, 1: Python, 2: Go, 3: Rust, 4: Java, 5: C#, 6: Ruby, 7: PHP, 8: Swift, 9: Kotlin. Evaluation criteria: team expertise (weight 9), ecosystem maturity (8), performance (7), operational cost (6), hiring pool (5). Weighted scores: Option A (Rust) — team expertise 8, ecosystem 9, performance 7, ops cost 7, hiring 8 = weighted 7.8. Option B (C#) — team expertise 6, ecosystem 7, performance 9, ops cost 6, hiring 5 = weighted 6.5. Decision: Option A based on team expertise and ecosystem maturity. Architectural invariant: all services in this domain use the same stack for operational simplicity.

Evolutionary architecture: user-profile space-based-architecture fitness functions. Fitness function 1: coupling — measure Afferent Coupling (Ca) and Efferent Coupling (Ce) per service. Threshold: Ce < 20, Ca < 30. Fitness function 2: cohesion — Lack of Cohesion of Methods (LCOM) per module. Threshold: LCOM < 0.8. Fitness function 3: dependency direction — layers must only depend on layers below. Enforced by architecture test (ArchUnit / Import Slicer). Fitness function 4: deployment independence — each service deployable without co-deployment of other services. Test: deploy single service in CI and verify all integration tests pass. Fitness function 5: response time — p99 latency under 200ms measured in production. Monitored via RED dashboard with SLO burn rate alerting.

Evolutionary architecture: audit actor-based fitness functions. Fitness function 1: coupling — measure Afferent Coupling (Ca) and Efferent Coupling (Ce) per service. Threshold: Ce < 20, Ca < 30. Enforced by architecture test (ArchUnit / Import Slicer). Fitness function 4: deployment independence — each service deployable without co-deployment of other services. Monitored via RED dashboard with SLO burn rate alerting.

Weighted scores: Option A (Python) — team expertise 8, ecosystem 9, performance 7, ops cost 7, hiring 8 = weighted 7.8. Option B (Rust) — team expertise 6, ecosystem 7, performance 9, ops cost 6, hiring 5 = weighted 6.5. Decision: Option A based on team expertise and ecosystem maturity. Architectural invariant: all services in this domain use the same stack for operational simplicity.

Evolutionary architecture: backup blackboard fitness functions. Fitness function 1: coupling — measure Afferent Coupling (Ca) and Efferent Coupling (Ce) per service. Threshold: Ce < 20, Ca < 30. Fitness function 2: cohesion — Lack of Cohesion of Methods (LCOM) per module. Threshold: LCOM < 0.8. Fitness function 3: dependency direction — layers must only depend on layers below. Enforced by architecture test (ArchUnit / Import Slicer). Fitness function 4: deployment independence — each service deployable without co-deployment of other services. Test: deploy single service in CI and verify all integration tests pass. Fitness function 5: response time — p99 latency under 200ms measured in production. Monitored via RED dashboard with SLO burn rate alerting.

Trade-off analysis: multi-tenant-saas for scheduling. Quality attributes: availability (99.99%), latency (p99 < 200ms), scalability (10k TPS), security (PCI-DSS Level 1), cost (<$50k/month). Architecture multi-tenant-saas scores: availability 9/10 (active-active multi-region), latency 8/10 (in-process calls vs network hops), scalability 7/10 (horizontal with partitioning), security 8/10 (defense-in-depth layers), cost 6/10 (infrastructure complexity). Alternative: simplified layered architecture scores availability 7/10, latency 9/10, scalability 5/10, security 7/10, cost 9/10. Recommendation: multi-tenant-saas for core domain, layered for bounded contexts where scalability is not critical.

Fitness function 3: dependency direction — layers must only depend on layers below. Enforced by architecture test (ArchUnit / Import Slicer). Fitness function 4: deployment independence — each service deployable without co-deployment of other services. Test: deploy single service in CI and verify all integration tests pass. Fitness function 5: response time — p99 latency under 200ms measured in production. Monitored via RED dashboard with SLO burn rate alerting.

Trade-off analysis: grid-computing for onboarding. Quality attributes: availability (99.99%), latency (p99 < 200ms), scalability (10k TPS), security (PCI-DSS Level 1), cost (<$50k/month). Architecture grid-computing scores: availability 9/10 (active-active multi-region), latency 8/10 (in-process calls vs network hops), scalability 7/10 (horizontal with partitioning), security 8/10 (defense-in-depth layers), cost 6/10 (infrastructure complexity). Alternative: simplified layered architecture scores availability 7/10, latency 9/10, scalability 5/10, security 7/10, cost 9/10. Recommendation: grid-computing for core domain, layered for bounded contexts where scalability is not critical.

Tech selection: payment on DigitalOcean with Python. Criteria: team expertise (9), ecosystem (8), performance (7), ops cost (6), hiring (5). Approval: CONDITIONAL — prototype proving boundary stability, cross-service query perf, deployment automation. Timeline: 6 weeks prototyping, 3 months implementation.

Fitness functions: payment event-driven architecture. FF1: coupling — Ca < 30, Ce < 20 per service. FF2: cohesion — LCOM < 0.8 per module. FF3: dependency direction — layers only depend down (ArchUnit test). FF4: deploy independence — single service deployable without co-deployment. FF5: p99 latency < 200ms in prod. Governance: architecture review board approves FF changes, monthly FF report in CI dashboard, FF regression fails build. FF evolution: functions added as architecture matures, retired when invariants proven.

Governance: architecture review board approves FF changes, monthly FF report in CI dashboard, FF regression fails build. FF evolution: functions added as architecture matures, retired when invariants proven.

Coupling: payment Java dependency analysis. Types ranked: content coupling (worst — module modifies internal data of another), common coupling (shared global state), external coupling (shared external format/interface), control coupling (passing flags to control behavior), stamp coupling (passing entire structure when only fields needed), data coupling (best — only necessary data). Target: < 10% content/common coupling, < 30% external/stamp, > 60% data coupling. Measure: Java dependency-cruiser / ArchUnit. Improvement: extract shared state to service, introduce interfaces at module boundaries.

Target: < 10% content/common coupling, < 30% external/stamp, > 60% data coupling. Measure: Java dependency-cruiser / ArchUnit. Improvement: extract shared state to service, introduce interfaces at module boundaries.

Target: < 10% content/common coupling, < 30% external/stamp, > 60% data coupling. Measure: Ruby dependency-cruiser / ArchUnit. Improvement: extract shared state to service, introduce interfaces at module boundaries.

Target: < 10% content/common coupling, < 30% external/stamp, > 60% data coupling. Measure: Swift dependency-cruiser / ArchUnit. Improvement: extract shared state to service, introduce interfaces at module boundaries.

Target: < 10% content/common coupling, < 30% external/stamp, > 60% data coupling. Measure: TypeScript dependency-cruiser / ArchUnit. Improvement: extract shared state to service, introduce interfaces at module boundaries.

Target: < 10% content/common coupling, < 30% external/stamp, > 60% data coupling. Measure: Go dependency-cruiser / ArchUnit. Improvement: extract shared state to service, introduce interfaces at module boundaries.

Data: DynamoDB cross-region replication. Cost impact: 2.5x infra cost for 10x reliability improvement. Measurement: SLO dashboard with burn rate alerts. Validation: quarterly durability exercise with chaos experiments.

Data: payment data architecture on OVH with Redis. Tiers: (1) OLTP Redis for transactions — strong consistency, partition by tenant_id. (2) Read replica for reporting — 1min stale, materialized views for aggregations. (3) Elasticsearch for search — indexed via CDC from Redis. (4) Data warehouse (Redshift / BigQuery / Snowflake) for analytics — batch loaded nightly. (5) S3 data lake for ML training — raw + processed data, lifecycle to glacier after 90 days. Schema: per-service schema ownership, shared schema only for reference data (countries, currencies).

(4) Data warehouse (Redshift / BigQuery / Snowflake) for analytics — batch loaded nightly. (5) S3 data lake for ML training — raw + processed data, lifecycle to glacier after 90 days. Schema: per-service schema ownership, shared schema only for reference data (countries, currencies).

(4) Data warehouse (Redshift / BigQuery / Snowflake) for analytics — batch loaded nightly. (5) S3 data lake for ML training — raw + processed data, lifecycle to glacier after 90 days. Schema: per-service schema ownership, shared schema only for reference data (countries, currencies).

(4) Data warehouse (Redshift / BigQuery / Snowflake) for analytics — batch loaded nightly. (5) S3 data lake for ML training — raw + processed data, lifecycle to glacier after 90 days. Schema: per-service schema ownership, shared schema only for reference data (countries, currencies).

(4) Data warehouse (Redshift / BigQuery / Snowflake) for analytics — batch loaded nightly. (5) S3 data lake for ML training — raw + processed data, lifecycle to glacier after 90 days. Schema: per-service schema ownership, shared schema only for reference data (countries, currencies).

(4) Data warehouse (Redshift / BigQuery / Snowflake) for analytics — batch loaded nightly. (5) S3 data lake for ML training — raw + processed data, lifecycle to glacier after 90 days. Schema: per-service schema ownership, shared schema only for reference data (countries, currencies).

(4) Data warehouse (Redshift / BigQuery / Snowflake) for analytics — batch loaded nightly. (5) S3 data lake for ML training — raw + processed data, lifecycle to glacier after 90 days. Schema: per-service schema ownership, shared schema only for reference data (countries, currencies).

Governance: payment architecture governance on Rust. Board: Staff Engineer, Architect, EM, SRE Lead. Review triggers: new service introduction, database technology change, inter-service communication pattern change, multi-team API contract, infrastructure provider change. Quorum: 3 of 4 members. Cadence: weekly async, monthly synchronous. Artifacts: ADR template (context, options, decision, consequences), RFC (design document, review comments, approval status), architecture decision log (searchable, tagged). Escalation: CTO for irreversible decisions or >$50k budget impact.

Migration: payment cloud migration to Linode. Phase 1 (assess): assess 50 services, 200 DB instances, 20 TB data. Target: Linode with MySQL managed service. Phase 2 (migrate): lift-and-shift for 30 services, re-architect for 20. Repository: Docker containers on Linode ECS/EKS/GKE, Python services compile to native binaries. Phase 3 (optimize): adopt Linode managed services (DB, cache, queue, monitoring), implement auto-scaling, reserved instances for baseline. Risk assessment: downtime during DB migration — use CDC for zero-downtime cutover. Timeline: 12 months.

Review: payment microkernel architecture review. Strengths: bounded context alignment with team topology, independent deployability per service, technology diversity justified. Concerns: (1) sync call chain depth of 4 violates resilience goal, (2) shared MySQL across 2 services creates coupling, (3) no circuit breaker on critical dependency admin. Recommendations: (1) introduce async event for depth > 3, (2) extract shared DB to service with SSE interface, (3) implement circuit breaker with fallback within 2 sprints. Decision: APPROVED WITH CONDITIONS — address within 1 quarter.


Review: inventory pipeline architecture review. Strengths: bounded context alignment with team topology, independent deployability per service, technology diversity justified. Concerns: (1) sync call chain depth of 4 violates resilience goal, (2) shared DynamoDB across 2 services creates coupling, (3) no circuit breaker on critical dependency analytics. Recommendations: (1) introduce async event for depth > 3, (2) extract shared DB to service with SOAP interface, (3) implement circuit breaker with fallback within 2 sprints. Decision: APPROVED WITH CONDITIONS — address within 1 quarter.
